newsitem.title: FRANCE: Outlook for French rate cuts brightens post Dublin.
newsitem.headline: Outlook for French rate cuts brightens post Dublin.

text.p: The Bank of France is likely to cut its official interest rates before the end of the year and may eliminate the spread between German rates over the next few months, economists said on Monday.

Growing confidence that European Union (EU) countries will launch a single currency on January 1, 1999, faltering French economic growth, low inflation and an uncertain economic outlook in Germany have combined recently to raise hopes the Bank of France will be able to further ease policy.

The most significant recent developments were statements of support for a stable franc by President Jacques Chirac last Thursday and the agreement at the weekend by EU nations to a budget discipline pact, both seen as major boosts to Europe's plans to launch Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Chirac's reaffirmation of French commitment to a tight franc/mark link was seen as killing off a resurgent debate in France about whether to devalue the franc launched by former President Valery Giscard d'Estaing.

The deal on the so-called stability pact lifted market confidence that France and Germany could find a way to compromise for the success of EMU and has allowed the franc to strengthen and market interest rates to fall.
Economists said the Bank of France is likely to capitalise on markets' serenity and resume small, steady interest rate cuts in the weeks ahead.

"The outlook for the Bank of France getting back on track has come closer really since the Chirac statements last Thursday and the accord in Dublin," said Iain Lindsay, bond strategist at Credit Lyonnais.
"It's almost dead certain they'll do 15 to 20 basis points because they have that much room anyway without going below German rates," bond strategist Sonja Gibbs of Nomura International said.
France's floor intervention rate is set at 3.20 percent, while the Bundesbank's securities repurchase rate, which sets the effective floor for European official interest rates, is now at 3.0 percent.

In what economists called a concrete sign that banks believe market rates will stay low in the coming months and that the road to EMU is smoothing, French commercial banks on Monday cut their base lending rates.
"This is clearly a sign of confidence linked to the stability pact and the outlook for rates," Credit Commercial de France economist Valerie Plagnol said of the base rate cuts.

Economists said the higher market confidence that EMU will launch on schedule may allow France to cut its rates below Germany's without any adverse effects like those that plagued France's past attempts to go through German rates.
"What's different this time is the market has become much more submitted to the prospect of EMU taking place," Lindsay said.

Economists said it might be some time before markets got used to this idea but that given recent falls in market rates in Italy and Spain, French rates should be able to sustain a negative spread to Germany.
"If the market can believe that Italy and Spain can narrow the spread as much as they have, then some parts of the French curve are undervalued," Gibbs said.
"French rates can converge and if fundamentals warrant and market psychology holds, they can even go below German rates," she said.
